The `terminal` commands of this lab are run when the book is built, in the

## Aims

- Launch your own workshop session on the Bioconductor Orchestra platform.
- Familiarize yourself with the `RStudio` interface.
- Learn how to use the terminal within `RStudio`.
- Learn how to find and download public single-cell data from the web.

:::

## Connect to RStudio Server on Orchestra

Most of single-cell RNA-seq analysis takes place either in `python` or in `R`.
Here, we focus on how to leverage `R` to investigate scRNAseq data.
`RStudio` is an `IDE` (Integrated Development Environment, in other words: a
nice graphical interface to run `R`-related commands).

For this workshop, every participant gets their own `RStudio Server` session,
running in the cloud from the **Docker image built from this book**, on the
[Orchestra platform](https://orchestraplatform.org/). Orchestra is an
open-source platform, supported by the Bioconductor community, which runs
workshop environments in the cloud: each participant gets their own, isolated
`RStudio` session, in their web browser. There is nothing to install on your
computer, and no password to type.

1. Open the Orchestra dashboard: **the link will be given by your instructors
   at the beginning of the workshop**.
2. Sign in with a Google account (any Google account works, either a personal
   Gmail address or an institutional account backed by Google).
3. Pick the **"Single-cell RNA-seq analysis with R/Bioconductor (Physalia 2026)"**
   workshop from the catalog and click on **Launch**. Starting the session can
   take a few minutes the first time (the status moves from `Pending` to
   `Starting` to `Ready`).
4. When it's `Ready`, click on **Open**: `RStudio` opens in a new tab of your
   browser, already logged in.

::: {.callout-warning icon='true'}
## Your session is temporary!

Every session has a time limit, shown as a countdown on its card in the
dashboard (you can extend it by clicking on `+1h`). **When a session expires
(or when you terminate it), everything in it is removed**, including the files
you created.

Download anything you want to keep (scripts, notebooks, results) before the end
of each day: in `RStudio`, tick the files in the `Files` pane, then click on
`More` > `Export...`.

If Orchestra is unavailable, you can run the same environment on your own
computer with Docker: see [Getting started](../getting-started.qmd).
:::

Notice how, once `RStudio` is open, there are multiple panels. Familiarize
yourself with the different panels.

The interactive `R` console is generally found in the bottom left corner of
`RStudio` (though it may be in another corner sometimes).
All the rest (history panel, environment panel, directory explorer panel,
editor panel) are extra features provided by `RStudio`.

::: {.callout-tip icon='true'}
## Some useful commands in `R`:

Within the `R` console, you can safely use `R`-dedicated commands.
Do you know the most common ones? The semantics are a different from the
`terminal` commands you may be used to...

```{r eval = FALSE, filename = "R"}
getwd() # equivalent of `pwd` in terminal
dir.create('~/data/') # equivalent of `mkdir ~/data/` in terminal
setwd("~/data/") # equivalent of `cd ~/data/` in terminal
list.files("~/data/") # equivalent of `ls` in terminal
download.file("...") # equivalent of `wget ...` in terminal
```
:::

## Use a terminal within RStudio

A general issue with bioinformatic analyses stems from the fact that nobody
works in the same environment:

- Are you working on Mac? Linux? Windows?
- Do you have a lot of computational power? Perhaps a GPU card?
- Are you connected to the Internet? With a fast connection? Are you working behind a proxy?
- Which versions of `R`, `Bioconductor` and of each package are installed?

To ensure that we are all working in the same environment, we all run the
**same Docker image**. A Docker image is a frozen, self-contained Linux system:
it ships a given version of `R`, `Bioconductor`, every `R` package and every
command-line tool used in this workshop, and even the datasets used in the
labs. Each participant runs their own copy of this image (a *container*) in
the cloud, so:

- **Everybody gets exactly the same software**, down to package versions;
- **Your session is yours**: you can install, modify or delete files without affecting anyone else;
- **Your session is temporary**: download the files you want to keep before the end of the workshop!

The easiest way to launch **`bash` commands from a terminal** is to do it
through `RStudio`: You can open up a `terminal` directly from within `RStudio`
as follows: go to `Tools` > `Terminal` > `New terminal`.
This should open up a new tab in the bottom left corner (next to the `R` console).

::: {.callout-warning icon='true'}
## `R console` versus `terminal`:

From here onwards, be sure you completely understand the difference between
**"`R console`"** and **"`terminal` (or `shell`)"**.
They are entirely different things, and can be both accessed within `RStudio`.
It is crucial you understand the difference between the two to not get
confused for the rest of the course.
:::

## Basic terminal commands

One can list files, download files, check help pages, ..., just like in `R`.

::: {.callout-note icon='true'}
## Code blocks and folders

On this page, each block of `bash` code is run in a new terminal, which starts
in your home folder (`~`): this is why some blocks start with `cd ~/data`. In
your own terminal, moving to `~/data` once is enough.
:::

- Check the your present directory

```{bash filename = "bash"}
pwd
```

- Check history (in your terminal, this lists the commands you typed; on this
  page, each block runs in a new terminal, so the history is empty)

```{bash filename = "bash"}
history
```

- put history into a `history.txt` file, in your home folder (`~`)

```{bash filename = "bash"}
history > ~/history.txt
```

- make a new folder called data (`-p`: do not complain if it already exists)

```{bash filename = "bash"}
mkdir -p ~/data
```

- Go to the new `data` directory

```{bash filename = "bash"}
cd ~/data
pwd
```

- move `history.txt` file into `data` directory

```{bash filename = "bash"}
cd ~/data
mv ../history.txt ./
ls -l
```

- check the help of the `wget` command (here, only its first 20 lines, with `head`)

```{bash filename = "bash"}
wget --help | head -n 20
```

::: {.callout-note icon='true'}
## Manual pages

On most Linux and macOS computers, `man <command>` shows the full manual page
of a command (e.g. `man wget`, hit `q` to exit). Like in most Docker images,
manual pages are not installed in the workshop environment: use
`<command> --help` instead.
:::

- check specific help for `samtools` command and subcommands

```{bash filename = "bash"}
samtools --help
samtools view --help | head -n 30
```

- redirect the help output into a file called `samtools-view-help.txt`

```{bash filename = "bash"}
cd ~/data
samtools view --help > samtools-view-help.txt
head -n 5 samtools-view-help.txt
```

- Download a file from Internet with `wget` (`-nv`: only print a summary
  line, rather than a progress bar)

```{bash filename = "bash", error = TRUE}
cd ~/data
wget -nv https://cf.10xgenomics.com/supp/cell-exp/cellranger-tiny-bcl-1.2.0.tar.gz
```

- List all files in a folder

```{bash filename = "bash"}
ls -lh ~/data/
```

::: {.callout-tip icon='true'}

## Single-cell RNA-seq datasets

> "This is a course about single-cell RNA-seq analysis, after all, so where is my data?"

Ok, **"your"** data is (most likely) yet to be sequenced! Or maybe you're
interested in digging already existing databases!

The [Human Cell Atlas data portal](https://data.humancellatlas.org/explore/projects)
and the [CZ CELLxGENE Discover](https://cellxgene.cziscience.com/datasets)
portal are probably good places to start digging, if you are interested in
mammal-related studies. For instance, let's say I am interested in epididymis
differentiation. Boom: here is an entry from the HCA focusing on epididymis:
[link to HCA data portal](https://data.humancellatlas.org/explore/projects/842605c7-375a-47c5-9e2c-a71c2c00fcad).

### Raw fastq reads from GEO

Here is the link to the actual paper studying epididymis:
[An atlas of human proximal epididymis reveals cell-specific functions and distinct roles for CFTR](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7471510/).

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Find and check out the corresponding `GEO` entries for this study. What type of
sequencing data is available?

::: {.callout-tip icon='true'}
Here is the link to the `GEO` page: [link](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE148963).
:::

:::
:::

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Can you find links to download the raw data from this paper?

:::
:::

There are several ways to find this information, e.g. `ffq` command line tool,
the web-based `sra-explorer` page ([here](https://sra-explorer.info/)), or the
[ENA browser](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/browser/home).
You generally will need the `GEO` corresponding ID or SRA project ID (e.g. `SRPxxxxxx`...).

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

The [`ffq` tool](https://github.com/pachterlab/ffq) from the Pachter lab is
already installed in your workshop session. Check `ffq` help and try fetching
the metadata of the sequencing run of sample `AXH009` (`GSM4486714`):
`SRR11575369`.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{bash filename = "bash", error = TRUE}
cd ~/data
ffq --help
ffq SRR11575369 > SRR11575369_ffq.json
head -n 30 SRR11575369_ffq.json
```

`ffq` returns the metadata of the run in `JSON` format: the experiment, study
and sample it belongs to, and the download links of its files.

::: {.callout-warning icon='true'}
## `429 Too Many Requests`

`ffq` queries the NCBI and ENA servers, which limit the number of requests
they accept from the same place: when all the participants of the workshop run
`ffq` at the same time, NCBI may reject some of the queries
(`ERROR 429 Client Error: Too Many Requests`), and `ffq` then writes an empty
file. Wait a little and try again or, if it keeps failing, use the copy of the
result provided in `~/Share/`:

```{bash filename = "bash"}
cd ~/data
## Use the copy in ~/Share/ if `ffq` failed (i.e. if SRR11575369_ffq.json is empty)
[ -s SRR11575369_ffq.json ] || cp ~/Share/SRR11575369_ffq.json ./
ls -l SRR11575369_ffq.json
```
:::

`ffq` can, in principle, also be queried with GEO accessions directly (e.g.
`ffq GSE148963`). With the current release of `ffq` (0.3.1), these queries
(as well as queries of SRA studies, `SRP...`) fail, as NCBI changed the GEO
web pages `ffq` reads. Queries of SRA runs (`SRR...`) work fine.

:::
:::

:::
:::

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Can you find the links to raw data associated with the `GSE148963` GEO ID?

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

`ffq` lists the download links of the files of the run, from several mirrors
(`ftp`: the ENA, `aws`, `gcp` and `ncbi`). You can use a `grep` command:
`grep` returns the lines which match a given pattern (e.g. a link...)!

```{bash filename = "bash", error = TRUE}
cd ~/data
grep '"url": "ftp://' SRR11575369_ffq.json
```

And with a bit of `sed` magick...

```{bash filename = "bash", error = TRUE}
cd ~/data
grep '"url": "ftp://' SRR11575369_ffq.json | sed 's,.*"ftp://,ftp://,' | sed 's,".*,,' > SRR11575369_fastqlist.txt
cat SRR11575369_fastqlist.txt
## `ffq` looks through the SRA/ENA databases to find metadata associated with the `SRR11575369` run (including download links)
## grep '"url": "ftp://' recovers the text lines that contain FTP download links
## the `sed` commands clean up the text lines
## the `wget` command downloads locally the links listed in the generated file (SRR11575369_fastqlist.txt)
# wget -i SRR11575369_fastqlist.txt ## Do not run, it would take too long (2 x 35 GB)...
```

:::
:::

:::
:::

Each of these two `fastq` files weighs ~35 GB: downloading them would take far
too long. Let's pretend we downloaded them with
`wget -i SRR11575369_fastqlist.txt`: their first 25,000 reads are available in
`~/Share/`.

```{bash filename = "bash"}
ls -lh ~/Share/SRR11575369_*.fq.gz
```

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}

Try and understand the structure of the `fq.gz` files. What is the meaning of
each line? What is the difference between the `_1` and `_2` files?

How many reads are there in each `fq.gz` file? And how long are they? Can you
get a summary of what is in these files? All of these questions can be quickly
answered using the [`seqkit`](https://bioinf.shenwei.me/seqkit/usage/) tool:

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{bash filename = "bash"}
zcat ~/Share/SRR11575369_1.fq.gz | head -n 8
zcat ~/Share/SRR11575369_2.fq.gz | head -n 8
```

```{bash filename = "bash"}
seqkit --help | head -n 30
seqkit stats --help | head -n 20
seqkit stats --quiet ~/Share/SRR11575369_*.fq.gz
```

::: {.callout-tip icon='true'}
## `zcat` on macOS

Running these commands on your own Mac? There, `zcat file.gz` looks for a
`file.gz.Z` file and fails: use `gzcat file.gz` (or `gunzip -c file.gz`)
instead. Reading a stream (`... | zcat`) works as on Linux.
:::

:::
:::

:::
:::

### Processed count matrices

Many times, researchers will provide a filtered count matrix when they publish
scRNAseq experiments (along with mandatory raw `fastq` data, of course). It's
way lighter than `fastq` reads, and you can go ahead with downstream analyses
a lot quicker. So how do you get these matrices? Human Cell Atlas Consortium
provides many processed datasets. For instance, in our case, the `A single cell
atlas of the human proximal epididymis reveals cell-type specific functions and
distinct roles for CFTR (Leir et al, 2020)` study is available at the
[following link](https://data.humancellatlas.org/explore/projects/842605c7-375a-47c5-9e2c-a71c2c00fcad).

GEO also provides access to both raw and processed files.

::: {.callout-question}
::: {.callout-note title="Question"}
Find GEO-hosted processed files for the `Leir et al` study.

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}
Check the [Geo Dataset search page](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gds/).

[Search for `Leir 2020 CFTF`](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gds/?term=leir+2020+CFTR).
You should find the [following entry](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE148963).

Scrolling down to the bottom of the page, there is a box labelled "Supplementary
data". Each sample (`GSM...`) also has its own supplementary files: for instance,
the processed files for sample `AXH009` are listed on the [GSM4486714 page](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSM4486714).
:::
:::

Download and check the content of the count matrix, the genes and the barcodes files.

What type of information does each file contain? How is it formatted? is it
easily imported in R?

::: {.callout-answer}
::: {.callout-note title="Answer" collapse="true"}

```{bash filename = "bash", error = TRUE}
cd ~/data
URL=https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/samples/GSM4486nnn/GSM4486714/suppl
for FILE in matrix.mtx genes.tsv barcodes.tsv; do
    wget -nv ${URL}/GSM4486714_AXH009_${FILE}.gz
done
ls -lh GSM4486714_AXH009_*
zcat GSM4486714_AXH009_genes.tsv.gz | head
zcat GSM4486714_AXH009_barcodes.tsv.gz | head
zcat GSM4486714_AXH009_matrix.mtx.gz | head
```

These three files are the standard output of `cellranger` (a "Matrix Market"
sparse matrix, see [Lab 2](Lab2_processingreads.qmd)): the `.mtx` file only
lists the non-zero entries of the count matrix, one per line, as
`<gene index> <cell index> <count>`, after a 3-line header. The genes and
barcodes files give the names of the rows and of the columns of the matrix.
We will see how to import them in `R` in [Lab 3](../day2/Lab3_Rbioc.qmd).

:::
:::

- How many cells were sequenced? How many genes were counted?
- Is it easy to interpret the count matrix? Why is it in such format?
- Comment on the file sizes between processed count matrix files and raw reads.

:::
:::
